articles.title: Clean Technology Advanced Packaging Market To 2035: Circular Economy Mandates Drive Material Innovation - News and Statistics - IndexBox
articles.summary: Clean Technology Advanced Packaging Market To 2035: Circular Economy Mandates Drive Material Innovation - News and Statistics  IndexBox
articles.full_text:
Amcor
Leader in recyclable & compostable solutions
According to the latest IndexBox report on the global Clean Technology Advanced Packaging market, the market enters 2026 with broader demand fundamentals, more disciplined procurement behavior, and a more regionally diversified supply architecture.
The World Clean Technology Advanced Packaging Market is entering a decisive phase as environmental regulation, brand sustainability commitments, and material science converge to reshape packaging design and procurement. This report defines the market as packaging solutions that reduce resource consumption, waste, and pollution across their lifecycle, including biodegradable and compostable materials, high-recycled-content packaging, reusable and refillable systems, plant-based and edible substrates, mono-material flexible formats, water-soluble polymers, and advanced clean-tech packaging materials.
Historical data from 2012 to 2025 shows a market transitioning from niche pilots to mainstream adoption, with growth accelerating as extended producer responsibility (EPR) schemes, recycled-content mandates, and corporate net-zero targets take effect. The forecast period 2026–2035 is expected to be defined by the scaling of collection and sorting infrastructure, the commercialization of new bio-based resins, and the standardization of design-for-recycling guidelines. Demand is broadening beyond food and beverage into e-commerce, consumer electronics, pharmaceuticals, and personal care, where packaging performance and sustainability credentials are increasingly co-required.
The competitive landscape features established material and packaging majors alongside agile specialists in bio-polymers and reusable systems. This analysis provides a data-driven view of market size, structure, demand drivers, restraints, end-use dynamics, and regional outlook to support strategic planning across the value chain.
The baseline scenario for the Clean Technology Advanced Packaging Market anticipates sustained expansion through 2035, with global value growing at a compound annual growth rate of 7.2% from 2026 to 2035. This outlook assumes continued tightening of packaging waste regulations in major economies, steady corporate adoption of recycled-content and reusable packaging targets, and gradual improvement in collection, sorting, and composting infrastructure. Volume growth will be led by mono-material flexible packaging and high-recycled-content rigid formats, which offer drop-in compatibility with existing filling lines and recycling streams.
Biodegradable and compostable materials will expand fastest in foodservice and agricultural applications where organic waste contamination is common, though growth will remain constrained by feedstock availability and industrial composting capacity. Reusable and refillable systems will gain traction in e-commerce and personal care, supported by deposit-return schemes and brand-led pilot programs. Regionally, Asia-Pacific will remain the largest and fastest-growing market, driven by manufacturing scale and rising domestic sustainability regulation, while Europe leads in regulatory stringency and recycled-content adoption.
North America will see accelerated investment in recycling infrastructure and bio-based material capacity. Latin America and the Middle East & Africa will grow from a smaller base, with adoption concentrated in export-oriented food and consumer goods supply chains. Key risks to the baseline include volatile bio-based feedstock prices, slower-than-expected infrastructure build-out, and potential regulatory delays, which could moderate growth by 1–2 percentage points.
Food and beverage remains the largest end-use sector for clean technology advanced packaging, driven by the need to balance shelf-life protection with recyclability and organic waste diversion. Currently, adoption is concentrated in fresh produce, bakery, foodservice, and beverage containers, where mono-material flexible packaging and recycled PET are gaining share. Through 2035, demand will be shaped by EPR fees that penalize non-recyclable formats, by retailer specifications for compostable or recycled-content packaging, and by consumer expectations for plastic-free or refillable options.
Key demand-side indicators include the share of foodservice packaging subject to single-use plastic bans, the volume of PET collected and recycled, and the number of industrial composting facilities accepting packaging. Growth will be fastest in compostable foodservice ware and high-recycled-content beverage bottles, while conventional multi-material laminates will decline. The sector's purchasing decisions will increasingly be coordinated with waste management infrastructure and regulatory timelines, making packaging design a strategic function rather than a procurement afterthought. Current trend: Steady expansion supported by fresh-food packaging, compostable foodservice items, and recycled-content beverage containers..
Major trends: Shift from multi-material laminates to mono-material flexible packaging for recyclability, Rising adoption of compostable foodservice ware in markets with organic waste collection, Increased use of recycled PET and recycled HDPE in beverage and dairy containers, Retailer-led specifications for recyclable or reusable packaging, and Growth of refill and reuse pilots in grocery and beverage retail.
Representative participants: Amcor plc, Sealed Air Corporation, Huhtamaki Oyj, Mondi Group, Berry Global Group, Inc, and Novamont S.p.A.
Consumer electronics packaging is undergoing a rapid shift toward fiber-based and recycled-content materials as brands respond to EPR regulations and consumer scrutiny of plastic waste. Currently, molded pulp trays, recycled paperboard, and recycled-content plastic bags are replacing expanded polystyrene and virgin plastic cushioning in many smartphone, accessory, and small appliance applications. Through 2035, demand will be driven by the need to protect high-value, miniaturized devices during e-commerce transit while meeting design-for-recycling and recycled-content targets.
Key indicators include the share of electronics packaging that is plastic-free, the recycled content of fiber-based materials, and the volume of packaging associated with e-commerce returns. Brands are also exploring reusable and refillable packaging for accessories and subscription services. The sector's high visibility makes it a testing ground for innovative materials, including water-soluble films for protective wraps and plant-based molded cushions. However, performance requirements for drop protection and static dissipation will limit substitution in high-end devices, sustaining demand for specialized clean-tech plastic formats.
Current trend: Growing demand for recycled-content and fiber-based protective packaging amid miniaturization and e-commerce returns..
Major trends: Replacement of expanded polystyrene with molded pulp and recycled fiber cushions, Adoption of recycled-content polyethylene bags and wraps for device protection, Design for disassembly and recycling of packaging components, Growth of reusable packaging for subscription and accessory programs, and Brand commitments to plastic-free packaging in flagship product lines.
Representative participants: Sealed Air Corporation, Sonoco Products Company, DS Smith Plc, Smurfit Kappa Group, Amcor plc, and Mondi Group.
Pharmaceutical packaging is a demanding segment where clean technology adoption is driven by regulatory requirements for patient safety, tamper evidence, and sustainability. Currently, adoption is concentrated in recyclable mono-material blister packs, recycled-content secondary cartons, and reusable transport containers for clinical trials and cold chain. Through 2035, demand will be shaped by the EU's packaging and packaging waste regulation, which will require recyclability and recycled content for pharmaceutical packaging, and by patient-centric designs such as refillable inhalers and reusable adherence packaging.
Key indicators include the recyclability rate of blister and bottle formats, the volume of recycled content in secondary packaging, and the growth of reusable shipping systems for temperature-sensitive biologics. The sector's stringent performance requirements mean that clean-tech materials must meet barrier, sterility, and stability standards, slowing substitution but creating higher-value opportunities for specialized converters. Collaboration between material suppliers, pharmaceutical companies, and waste management firms will be critical to closing the loop for blister packs and other complex formats. Current trend: Regulatory pressure and patient-centric design drive adoption of recyclable and reusable packaging systems..
Major trends: Development of recyclable mono-material blister packs, Increased use of recycled content in secondary cartons and leaflets, Growth of reusable and temperature-controlled shipping containers for clinical trials, Patient-centric refill and reuse systems for inhalers and adherence packaging, and Regulatory pressure for recyclability under EU packaging rules.
Representative participants: Amcor plc, Constantia Flexibles Group GmbH, Huhtamaki Oyj, Sonoco Products Company, Berry Global Group, Inc, and Mondi Group.
E-commerce and logistics is the fastest-growing end-use sector for clean technology advanced packaging, driven by the exponential growth of parcel volumes and the need to reduce packaging waste per shipment. Currently, adoption is led by recycled-content paper mailers, mono-material plastic mailers, and reusable shipping containers for business-to-business and closed-loop retail. Through 2035, demand will be shaped by lightweighting targets, EPR fees that penalize non-recyclable formats, and the scaling of reusable packaging-as-a-service models. articles.title: EUDR Compliance Readiness in 2026 – Key Lessons for Forest Products Companies - ResourceWise
articles.summary: EUDR Compliance Readiness in 2026 – Key Lessons for Forest Products Companies  ResourceWise
articles.full_text:
With the European Union Deforestation Regulation (EUDR) nearing implementation, forest products companies must ask whether their compliance processes can provide the evidence needed to demonstrate due diligence.
In 2026, ResourceWise hosted a four-part EUDR Readiness Briefing Series to help industry professionals track regulatory developments, address operational challenges, and assess supply chain traceability.
A key takeaway: readiness requires more than collecting supplier information. Companies must verify material origins, link them to products and shipments, and maintain defensible documentation.
Companies with existing EUDR solutions or internal processes should identify gaps before they affect compliance reporting or EU market access.
A recurring theme was the distinction between established responsible-sourcing practices and the specific evidence EUDR requires.
Forest products companies have long used certification, chain-of-custody systems, legality assessments, and supplier documentation to support sustainable sourcing. These programs offer a valuable foundation but do not, on their own, prove EUDR compliance. Companies must demonstrate that covered products meet the regulation’s deforestation-free and legality requirements, supported by due diligence information.
This means evaluating whether existing programs can provide geolocation evidence, risk assessments, and links between production areas and products sold in the EU. Companies may not need to rebuild their sustainability programs, but must ensure they provide EUDR’s specific, verifiable evidence.
Geolocation was a major operational challenge discussed in the webinars. Collecting coordinates is a starting point, but does not establish the full production area or verify accuracy.
Under EUDR, companies must provide geolocation for relevant production plots. Depending on plot size and type, this may require polygons rather than a single point. For forest-product companies with extensive supplier networks, obtaining accurate polygons can create significant administrative work—especially when suppliers have varying technical capabilities or information must be gathered across many harvest sites.
Webinar discussions emphasized moving beyond data collection to processes that:
Having geolocation data is not the same as reliably verifying it. For companies assessing EUDR readiness, existing systems may collect coordinates but lack efficient ways to validate them or use them in downstream reporting.
Unlike supply chains with products traceable to a single production site, forest products pass through multiple stages before reaching their destination. Wood may be harvested, transported to a sawmill, turned into chips or residuals, sent to a pulp mill, and made into paper or packaging. Materials from different origins may be mixed during storage, processing, and manufacturing, making it difficult to link products or shipments to their source areas.
ResourceWise experts emphasized that effective traceability must reflect how wood and fiber move through the supply chain, linking harvest origins, supplier transactions, manufacturing facilities, and finished-product shipments. Sawmill and harvest residuals are especially important: they make up a substantial share of many supply chains, but movement through intermediaries can complicate origin reporting.
EUDR traceability must reflect real production and sourcing practices, not assume a simple path from raw materials to finished products. Companies with existing compliance systems should ask: Can they track mixed fiber, residuals, and multiple sourcing locations without significant manual work?
EUDR readiness depends on supplier participation across the forest products value chain. Even companies with established compliance systems may struggle if suppliers cannot provide consistent, usable information.
ResourceWise's implementation experience shows supplier data availability improving as companies prepare and origin requests become more common. But collecting data is only part of the process: companies also need reliable ways to transmit, validate, organize, and update records.
In the third briefing, Barry Parrish, ResourceWise’s Director of Sustainability, highlighted the value of supplier communication, training, and structured project management. Based on ResourceWise’s experience, communicating requirements, training suppliers to submit data, and collecting geolocation information can take about two months.
Companies should assess not just whether they have the required data, but how efficiently they can obtain missing information and maintain complete records. Those managing extensive supplier networks should ask:
These operational factors determine whether compliance remains manageable as reporting volumes grow.
A final theme was the need to move beyond collecting compliance data and integrate it into daily operations. Accurate harvest-area data, risk assessments, and supplier records must support EUDR-regulated products and shipments by linking origin details to production and shipment records and due diligence documents.
The webinars also discussed the EU's TRACES-based EUDR Information System for submitting due diligence statements. Companies must make these reporting processes operational before commercial shipments require them, including for materials produced before the regulation applies but placed on the EU market afterward. Compliance should therefore inform inventory and shipment planning, not just production.
Overall, EUDR readiness must cover the entire workflow, from supplier data collection to final compliance documentation.
The four-part series reinforced an important distinction between having an EUDR compliance strategy from having a process that reliably supports implementation.
Companies with compliance systems should assess how they perform across real supply chains: Can geolocation be verified? Do origins remain traceable through processing and mixing? Can evidence be linked to shipments and reporting requirements?
They should also evaluate maintenance demands. Workflows reliant on manual data collection, spreadsheets, or repeated supplier requests may be hard to scale.
Rather than simply asking whether a solution exists, forest products companies should ask whether it produces accurate, defensible information efficiently and consistently.
ResourceWise developed Forest Trackt to address the specific traceability and geolocation challenges found throughout forest products supply chains.
The platform helps companies collect supplier information, generate harvest-area polygons through geospatial change detection, connect origin data to downstream products and shipments, and prepare compliance-ready reporting.
These capabilities are particularly relevant for companies managing extensive supplier networks, sawmill residuals, and complex fiber flows.
For organizations reviewing existing EUDR processes, Forest Trackt offers an opportunity to evaluate where greater automation, traceability, and data verification could strengthen readiness.

articles.title: Microplastics Policy Patchwork Challenges Plastics Industry - PlasticsToday
articles.summary: Microplastics Policy Patchwork Challenges Plastics Industry  PlasticsToday
articles.full_text:
Experts Unpack Shifting Microplastics Rules Across US
A B&C webinar examined microplastics' murky definitions, emerging US federal and state regulations, and EPR compliance challenges facing plastics manufacturers.
Plastic manufacturers and processors are juggling the implications of a quickly changing microplastics policy landscape, as microplastics' place on the world stage of public and political scrutiny has resulted in a flood of emerging legal and regulatory actions at the international, national, and state levels.
To help affected companies make sense of it all, Washington, D.C.-based Bergeson and Campbell(B&C)hosted the "Plastics and Policy: Microplastics, EPR, and Other Emerging Trends" webinar.
"These are issues that will challenge every entity in the supply chain and raise really interesting scientific, constitutional, legal, and policy issues for years to come," said B&C Managing Partner Lynn L. Bergeson.
No universal definition, but plenty to think about
There is no globally accepted definition for microplastics, but a common core definition is forming, according to B&C Senior Toxicologist and Regulatory Scientist Lindsay A. Holden, PhD.
A microplastic is generally described as a solid plastic or polymer particle that could be a fragment or a fiber and may be as big as 5 mm. Primary microplastics are intentionally produced in a small size, like a microbead or plastic pellet. Secondary microplastics are breakdown products of larger plastic products.
"… definitions of microplastics differ, not at that top end of the size definition, but rather that lower size boundary," Holden said.
There is no consensus on how small a microplastic can be. The US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) and the State of California Water Board set the lower limit at 1 nm, but EPA makes a specific identification of a nanoplastic as anything that is less than 1 micron (µm). The International Organization for Standardization (ISO) defines a microplastic as 1 µm up to 1 mm, and a large microplastic as 1 mm to 5 mm. In Canada, a microplastic is 5 mm or less, without a formal nanoplastic threshold, she said.
The scope of how to define microplastics also differs across countries and organizations.
While the EPA and Canada define microplastics based on broad, size-based concepts, the main EU law protecting human health and the environment from chemical risks — the Registration, Evaluation, Authorization and Restriction of Chemicals (REACH) regulation — applies specific criteria for synthetic polymers, including tests for solubility, degradability, and composition, according to Holden.
Dimensionality is another difference, as some definitions are based on the size of a particle and do not discern between a particle and a fiber.
"The definition of what constitutes a fiber microplastic also changes across jurisdictions," Holden said.
Regardless of the exact definition, the most important aspects of microplastics are how a polymer's size, shape, and composition affect health and the environment. On those fronts, questions remain.
Potential hazards from microplastics are not characterized enough in people or the environment to truly understand "almost anything" about the implications of dose-response relationships, according to Holden.
"What we do know and have pretty strong consensus on is that exposure to microplastics is ubiquitous because of their presence in the environment," she said. "This is despite every effort that we've made thus far to keep plastics out of the environment. We're just not doing a perfect job of maintaining plastics through recycling programs. So, hazard is undefined, exposure is established, and risk is the combination of those two."
People in the plastics industry need to think about how to track and manage the evolving jurisdictional definitions of microplastics while incorporating changing and shifting recyclability requirements, Holden said.
"How do you label your product, whether or not it's recyclable? Then … is there going to be source attribution to those microplastics in the environment? That's very difficult to do, but there is public pressure on finding a solution for microplastics in the environment. Then, of course, [there's] compliance," Holden said.
US regulatory updates
Microplastics are coming into focus at the federal level.
"In addition to programs and initiatives that are specifically targeting microplastics, there are a range of ongoing policy approaches that more indirectly implicate and impact the plastics industry as a whole," said B&C Associate Catherina D. Narigon.
There are only a few overarching federal frameworks that target microplastics.
"The MicroBead Free Waters Act of 2015 is the singular law that has been passed federally that targets microplastics, but this law is limited in scope to cosmetic products, such as face wash and toothpaste, and therefore does not regulate microplastics as a class more broadly," Narigon said.
Two bipartisan research bills introduced in 2025 have not yet moved far along. However, both the Microplastics Safety Act and the Plastic Health Research Act were introduced with the intention of gathering information about microplastics and funding research initiatives to collect data that could guide future regulatory decisions. This indicates a growing interest at the federal level to potentially create laws that oversee microplastics, Narigon said.
Federal agencies have taken more interest in microplastics in recent years. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) is researching and tracking microplastics in oceans and waterways. Under the current Trump administration, the EPA and the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) have taken a stance against microplastics as a health risk and hazard.
"In April of this year, EPA and HHS released a joint statement about their respective commitments to reducing microplastics in drinking water and protecting residents and constituents who have contaminated water. EPA has had some misalignment between these statements and actual action, which has been interesting," Narigon said.
Notably, EPA's sixth Unregulated Contaminant Monitoring Rule (UCMR 6) was promulgated without including microplastics, and the UCMR is a necessary steppingstone to regulation under the Safe Drinking Water Act, she said.
At the state level, the microplastics regulatory scenario is more active.
Many states have enacted laws or programs specific to microplastics, but they vary state by state in a kind of jurisdictional patchwork. These laws are surfacing through measures such as plastic bag bans aimed at preventing single-use plastic bags and similar products from degrading into microplastics when discarded into the environment, Narigon explained.
"Many states have passed research bills that seek to gather information about the presence of microplastics in the environment or in the human body [with plans to use the information] to make regulatory decisions," Narigon said.
Product labeling laws are another piece of the puzzle. While states do not always take an approach specific to microplastics, plastics and microplastics are indirectly regulated and limited through labeling laws and similar initiatives, Narigon said.
Example in the Golden State
California's Truth in Recycling law, or Senate Bill 343, is an example of this. The law would heavily restrict which products can be labeled as recyclable.
"This law would have been effective as of Sunday, October 4 … but due to ongoing litigation and a preliminary injunction in the case, California is currently enjoined from enforcing the law," Narigon said.
While the purpose of the law is consumer protection, in practice, it creates a "really funky obstacle course for manufacturers and producers doing business in multiple states because many states expressly require recycling language and symbology on products that are prohibited from that language in California," Narigon said.
In another labeling law example, New Mexico's PFAS (per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances) Protection Act, passed during the 2025 legislative session, phases out consumer products with intentionally added PFAS, according to the New Mexico Environment Department.
"Starting January 1, 2027, products such as cookware, food packaging, dental floss, juvenile products, and firefighting foam are banned. On January 1, 2028, it expands to include carpets, cleaning items, cosmetics, fabrics, feminine hygiene products, textiles, ski wax, and upholstered furniture. By January 1, 2032, virtually all nonexempt products containing intentionally added PFAS are prohibited unless deemed a 'currently unavoidable use' by the Environmental Improvement Board," according to the New Mexico Environment Department's website.
Here, too, a federal court issued a preliminary injunction barring New Mexico from requiring businesses to label products containing PFAS with a disclosure, offering companies a reprieve.
Narigon pointed out that New Mexico uses an unclear and broad definition of PFAS that includes products and plastics not necessarily thought of as traditional PFAS.
Then there is extended producer responsibility (EPR), which has affected the plastics industry over the last several years.
"At a high level, EPR is a product stewardship policy that moves managerial and financial responsibility for product end-of-life management from the end user or municipality upstream onto the manufacturer or producer of that product. Seven US states have enacted programs for plastics and packaging under EPR," Narigon said.
At a high level, EPR programs in California, Colorado, Maryland, Maine, Minnesota, Oregon, and Washington are similar in that the producer — the obligated party under the law — is defined relatively similarly across each program, she said.

articles.title: Four years after the promises of Cop15, our biodiversity targets are slipping away - The Guardian
articles.summary: Four years after the promises of Cop15, our biodiversity targets are slipping away  The Guardian
articles.full_text:
The world has lost its way on nature once again. Next week, biodiversity Cop17 begins in Yerevan, Armenia, and expectations are low. Very low.
Almost four years ago, governments reached an historic agreement at the biodiversity Cop15 to halt the destruction of Earth’s ecosystems – to rapturous applause in Montreal, Canada. I still remember the excitement in the hall in the early hours of that freezing December morning.
Governments had never met a self-mandated target on biodiversity loss, but there was a sense after the Covid-19 pandemic that this time really would be different. The 23-point deal included targets to protect 30% of the planet for nature, restore 30% of the planet’s degraded terrestrial, inland water, coastal and marine ecosystems, and tackle $500bn of environmentally damaging subsidies. Almost every country in the world, apart from the US and the Vatican, backed it.
Yes, the agreement was flawed, and barely matched what the science tells us we need to do to stop biodiversity loss. But it was a serious, considered plan to tackle the underlying causes of the largest loss of life since the dinosaurs (this time, humans are the asteroid).
Since then, though, action has fallen short. More on why that is, what it means and what is at stake at Cop17, after this week’s climate headlines.
Essential reads
- A perfect storm: how the super El Niño is devastating the fishing industry
- ‘We need less point scoring’: What party conference season taught us about UK climate action
- ‘I didn’t want to write about this’: the man who first saw chimps waging civil war
In focus
The summit in Yerevan is about assessing progress towards the targets, and the scorecard does not look good. In preparatory meetings governments have acknowledged (pdf) that they are way off track from meeting any of the targets. The traffic-light system used to rate actions towards the targets from countries is awash with yellow, orange and red.
“Unless collective implementation accelerates rapidly, the 2030 targets and mission will not be achieved,” the pre-Cop17 report reads. “Parties and other actors have taken action to address all 23 targets; however, no target presents a fully positive picture. The available evidence indicates that there are gaps in the collective progress. Without urgently addressing these gaps and barriers, it will not be possible to meet the 2030 targets and mission, in turn placing achievement of the 2050 goals and vision [to live in harmony with nature] in jeopardy.”
This time, it is hard to be too angry with some governments. Countries including Kazakhstan have used the agreement to drive a major rewilding effort, bringing back the caspian tiger. The EU did attempt to enact the targets with the nature restoration law – but it quickly became a culture-wars issue. Swathes of the world, though, have turned against action on the environment.
Donald Trump’s return to the White House has been catastrophic for the conservation sector, caught in his administration clampdown on the climate and “woke” policies. Through USAID and partner organisations, the US government provided, on average, 12.1% of the world’s biodiversity funding between 2015 and 2022, according to the OECD. Almost all of that has gone, hitting everything from anti-rhino poaching initiatives in east Africa, to efforts to combat illegal fishing in the Galápagos.
Power has also drained out of multilateral organisations such as the UN. Tech billionaires and the architects of AI are more powerful than many countries. Trump’s second term has seen a return to might-is-right politics that is dismissive of the international cooperation needed to make an agreement like this a reality.
So what next? Cop17 in Armenia is likely to be a moment where the calamity of the last four years crystallises – and governments must try to pick up the pieces.
“There’s a massive gap between countries agreeing to do something and actually doing it,” says Zac Goldsmith, who was UK environment minister when that landmark Cop15 deal was reached in 2022. “That’s where we are today.”
